summary: Describes using AES in Cipher Block Chaining mode, with an explicit initialization vector, to provide confidentiality in IPsec ESP. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IPsec needs a way to scramble data. This memo says how to use a well-known scrambler called AES in a chained mode, so identical data does not look the same twice.

questions: how does esp use aes cbc
what size iv does aes-cbc esp use
what key sizes does aes cbc ipsec support
subtitle: How to use AES in CBC mode, with a fresh random IV in every packet, to encrypt IPsec ESP traffic.

tldr.problem: NIST had selected AES as the successor to DES, and IPsec needed a defined way to use it for confidentiality in the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).
tldr.mechanism: ESP carries a 16-octet explicit IV followed by AES-CBC ciphertext, padded to a multiple of 16 octets. Keys are 128 bits by default, with 192 and 256 optional, and the IV must be random and unpredictable.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives IANA identifiers for IKE negotiation and test vectors for checking implementations. The authors expected AES to become a MUST-implement ESP cipher.

today: RFC 3602 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why AES for IPsec
sections.content:
NIST selected the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), formerly known as Rijndael, as the successor to DES after a four-year open competition. The RFC lists the selection criteria, including security, being publicly disclosed, royalty-free availability worldwide, a block size of at least 128 bits and key sizes of 128, 192 and 256 bits.

The IETF IPsec Working Group intended that AES would eventually become the default IPsec ESP cipher and gain the status of MUST be included in compliant implementations. This document specifies how AES is used inside ESP.
sections.plainLanguage: A big contest picked the best secret-code machine, called AES. This memo says how IPsec should use the winner.

sections.title: AES Mode, Key Sizes and Rounds
sections.content:
The RFC specifies CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode. It is well understood and is already required for the other ESP ciphers. CBC needs an initialization vector (IV) the same size as the cipher block. The IV is XOR'd with the first plaintext block before encryption. Each later plaintext block is XOR'd with the previous ciphertext block first. A random IV keeps packets with identical data from producing identical ciphertext.

AES supports three key sizes. 128 bits is the default and all implementations MUST support it; 192 and 256 bits are optional (MAY). The number of rounds is fixed per key size: 10 for 128 bits, 12 for 192 bits and 14 for 256 bits.

No weak keys were known for AES at the time of writing. If any are found, they should be checked for with manual key management but not with dynamic key management such as IKE.
sections.plainLanguage: Each block of the message is mixed with the scrambled block before it, like links in a chain. The key size is how long the secret password is.

sections.title: The ESP Payload and Padding
sections.content:
The ESP payload is the IV followed by the raw ciphertext. The IV is 16 octets, the same as the AES block size, and the encrypted payload is a multiple of 16 octets.

The IV MUST be chosen at random and MUST be unpredictable. Implementations MUST NOT use a counter or other low-Hamming-distance source for IVs. Because every datagram carries its own IV, each one can be decrypted even if others are dropped or reordered.

AES uses a 16-octet block, so padding MUST be added, as specified in the ESP RFC, so that the data to encrypt (including the Pad Length and Next Header fields) is a multiple of 16 octets. This also keeps those two fields right-aligned in a 4-octet word, so no extra alignment padding is needed. Additional padding MAY be included if the 16-octet block size is kept.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet comes with its own random starting number written on the outside, so the receiver can unlock any packet even if others got lost.

sections.title: Keying Material and IKE
sections.content:
The key exchange protocol must supply at least as many bits of keying material as the key size. The cipher key is taken from the first bits of that material, as many as the key size requires.

For IKE, IANA assigned Encryption Algorithm ID 7 for AES-CBC in Phase 1 and ESP Transform Identifier 12 (ESP_AES) in Phase 2. Because AES has variable key lengths, the Key Length attribute MUST be specified in both phases.

On hashing, HMAC-SHA-1 and HMAC-MD5 were considered strong enough both to generate 128-bit AES keys in IKE and to authenticate ESP packets encrypted with 128-bit keys. The newer SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 give outputs sized for all three AES key sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers agree on a secret key, they also agree on the code number for AES and how long the key is.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC includes eight test cases so implementers can check their work. The first four encrypt 16, 32, 48 and 64 bytes (one to four blocks) with a 128-bit key, each giving key, IV, plaintext and ciphertext. The last four show sample ESP packets using AES-CBC.

Case 5, for example, is a transport-mode ESP packet carrying a ping from 192.168.123.3 to 192.168.123.100 with SPI 4321. The test cases were verified with two independent implementations: the NIST AES-CBC reference implementation and one from the authors of Rijndael.
sections.plainLanguage: These are practice problems with the right answers, so you can check that your own scrambler gives the same results.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations are encouraged to use the largest key sizes they can, taking performance into account on both sides of a secure channel. A 128-bit key is considered secure for the foreseeable future.

The RFC points to outside work on why random IV values are necessary, and refers readers to the AES specification for further security considerations. IANA assigned Encryption Algorithm ID 7 and ESP Transform Identifier 12.
sections.plainLanguage: A longer secret password is safer, but it takes more work to use. A medium-length one is already strong enough.
